name: Motion function
controls: What each movement does for the viewer: its job in the communication, independent of how it feels (motion language) or how scenes connect (transitions).
question: What jobs should the motion do for the viewer?
notes: Motion function classifies movement by purpose, following the functional-motion thinking in Material Design's motion guidance, Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and Issara Willenskomer's UX in Motion principles; the labels here are a practical synthesis, not a single standard. One tween usually serves several functions at once (a card that expands both transforms and shows hierarchy); pick the functions the piece must prioritize and let them decide what moves, while motion language decides how. Rule of thumb for product motion: every movement should serve at least one function other than 'decorate', and decorative motion should never compete with a functional one in the same frame. Enter/exit describe presence; reveal/conceal describe visibility of content that already exists in the layout; transform/morph describe one element changing; the 'show ...' functions describe what the change explains.

options.what: Brings an element into the frame or scene where it did not exist before.
options.looks: An element appears via a mask rise, scale settle, slide from an edge or a draw-on.
options.motion: Ease-out curves; direction implies origin (from the right means it came from 'next').
options.use: Every scene: headlines, cards, UI panels, icons.
options.conveys: Arrival and origin; the direction and style of entry say where the thing came from and how important it is.
options.vs: Reveal uncovers something that was conceptually already there (behind a mask or layer); enter implies the element arrives from elsewhere.
options.prompt: Give every element an intentional entrance whose direction matches its origin (content from the next step enters from the right, dropped items from above); use the motion language's enter ease; avoid fade plus 20px upward slide; the hero element enters last or largest.

options.what: Removes an element from the frame or scene.
options.looks: Elements slide out, collapse, wipe off or cut away, usually faster than they arrived.
options.motion: Ease-in curves; exits typically 60-70% of the entrance duration; direction implies destination.
options.use: Scene changes, dismissing notifications, removing completed items, clearing the stage for the hero.
options.conveys: Completion, dismissal, where the thing went.
options.vs: Conceal hides content that remains in the layout (a panel collapsing back under a header); exit removes the element entirely.
options.prompt: Exit elements faster than they entered (about 0.6 times the entrance duration) with the motion language's exit ease, moving toward their logical destination (completed items off to the left, dismissed toasts back to their edge); exit secondary elements before the hero.

options.what: Uncovers content that was hidden behind a mask, layer or crop, as if lifting a curtain.
options.looks: clip-path wipes, masks opening from center, layers sliding away to expose what is beneath, type rising from behind a baseline mask.
options.motion: clip-path inset or circle tweens, yPercent 100 to 0 inside overflow-hidden wrappers, sliding cover plates.
options.use: Headline reveals, product unveilings, before/after, feature highlights, logo reveals.
options.conveys: Discovery, anticipation paid off, something worth waiting for.
options.vs: Enter implies movement from elsewhere; reveal keeps the content fixed and moves the mask. Reveal is the most common alternative to generic fade-ins.
options.prompt: Reveal content by moving a mask, not the content: wrap text lines in overflow-hidden containers and rise them from yPercent 100 to 0, or animate clip-path inset(0 100% 0 0) to inset(0 0 0 0) left to right; for hero objects open a circle(0% at 50% 50%) clip-path to circle(75%).

options.what: Hides content by covering, masking or collapsing it while it conceptually stays in place.
options.looks: A mask closes, a cover plate slides over, a panel folds shut, a blur or dim layer overlays.
options.motion: Reverse of reveal: clip-path closes, wrappers collapse height, overlays slide in.
options.use: Hiding complexity, closing drawers, transitioning attention away, setting up a second reveal.
options.conveys: Simplification, closure, focus elsewhere; can build mystery before a new reveal.
options.vs: Exit removes the element from the world; conceal keeps it available, just out of view.
options.prompt: Conceal by closing a mask in the direction opposite to its reveal (clip-path inset back to 100% on the right), or by collapsing height to 0 on the container while children stay put; dim unimportant layers to 20-30% opacity with a solid overlay rather than removing them.

options.what: Changes an element's size, position, rotation or layout while it remains recognizably the same object.
options.looks: A card grows into a full panel, a button stretches into a progress bar, a grid reflows into a list.
options.motion: Shared-element FLIP-style tweens of x/y/width/height/borderRadius; ease-in-out; children re-layout inside.
options.use: UI state changes, card expansion, layout shifts, temporal composition (centered hero to grid to full-screen).
options.conveys: Continuity of identity: this is the same thing, now in a new role.
options.vs: Morph changes the shape into a different shape (circle to check mark); transform keeps the shape family and changes geometry or layout.
options.prompt: Transform elements in place instead of swapping them: measure start and end boxes and tween x, y, width, height and borderRadius together with the move ease (FLIP technique), keeping the element's fill and content continuous so the viewer tracks one object through the change.

options.what: Interpolates one shape into a different shape so a form turns into another form.
options.looks: A circle becomes a check mark, a play icon becomes a pause icon, a blob becomes a logo, a bar chart becomes a line.
options.motion: SVG path interpolation (MorphSVG or matching point counts), clip-path polygon tweens, border-radius changes.
options.use: Icon state changes, logo reveals, concept transitions, data changing form.
options.conveys: Transformation of meaning: one idea becomes another.
options.vs: Transform changes geometry but not identity; morph changes the form itself. As a scene transition, see transitions/morph.
options.prompt: Morph shapes by interpolating SVG paths with equal point counts (or GSAP MorphSVGPlugin) or clip-path polygons with matching vertex counts, over 500-900ms with an in-out ease; keep color and position continuous so the form change reads as one object becoming another.

options.what: Draws extra weight to an element already on screen without moving it elsewhere.
options.looks: Pulse, color fill, underline sweep, scale bump, glow, weight increase on a variable font.
options.motion: Short scale bumps (1 to 1.06 to 1), underline scaleX draws, color tweens, variable-font weight tweens.
options.use: Key words in kinetic type, prices and stats, the feature being discussed, CTA buttons.
options.conveys: Importance, 'this matters'.
options.vs: Direct attention moves the viewer's gaze to something (via camera, arrows, dimming); emphasize intensifies what they are already looking at.
options.prompt: Emphasize in place: sweep a 2-4px accent underline under the key word (scaleX 0 to 1 from the left), or tween its color to the accent, or bump scale 1 to 1.06 and back over 300-450ms; emphasize one element per beat only.

options.what: Moves the viewer's gaze to a specific place in the frame.
options.looks: Camera push toward a region, surrounding content dims or blurs, arrows or cursors travel to the target, a spotlight mask.
options.motion: Directional movement that points: leading lines, a travelling cursor, a zoom, a spotlight clip-path.
options.use: UI walkthroughs, dashboards, dense screens, callouts in product demos.
options.conveys: Guidance, clarity in complexity.
options.vs: Emphasize changes the target itself; direct attention changes the context (camera, dimming, pointers) around it.
options.prompt: Direct the eye before the target changes: dim everything except the target to 30% (overlay with a spotlight cut-out via clip-path or mask), push the camera 10-20% toward it, or travel a cursor or arrow along a curved path to it; arrive 200-300ms before the target's own animation starts.

options.what: Shows that an input was received: a response to a click, tap, keystroke or drag.
options.looks: Button press-down, ripple, toggle knob travel, field focus ring, character appearing on keystroke.
options.motion: Immediate response (under 100ms start), short press scale 0.96 and release, ripples expanding from the input point.
options.use: UI interaction demos, cursor-driven product films, micro-interaction showcases.
options.conveys: Responsiveness, a product that listens.
options.vs: Show state change is the result (toggle now on); feedback is the acknowledgement of the input (the press itself).
options.prompt: Acknowledge every simulated input instantly: at the click frame scale the pressed control to 0.96 for 80-120ms and release; expand a ripple circle from the cursor point (scale 0 to 2.5 with the opacity falling to 0); show focus rings as a 2px outline drawing in.

options.what: Links an action to its consequence so the viewer sees one thing causing another.
options.looks: A click sends a pulse down a connector line into a result card, a toggle recolors a chart, an input flows into an output.
options.motion: Sequential timing with a visible carrier (a pulse, particle or line) travelling from cause to effect; the effect starts as the carrier arrives.
options.use: Input to output demos, automation and workflow products, AI generation, integrations.
options.conveys: Power and control, how the product works.
options.vs: Show relationship shows two things are connected; cause and effect shows direction and consequence in time.
options.prompt: Make cause precede effect visibly: trigger (click or input) first, then a carrier (a 4-8px dot or a dashed line drawing) travels from cause to effect over 300-600ms, and the effect animates exactly on arrival; never start the effect before the cause completes.

options.what: Uses order, timing and scale of motion to tell the viewer what is primary, secondary and tertiary.
options.looks: Hero arrives first and largest, supporting items follow with smaller motion; parents move before children.
options.motion: Order and delay (parent then children), larger travel and longer duration for primary items, tighter stagger for tertiary.
options.use: Landing-page heroes, feature grids, dashboards, lists, org or system diagrams.
options.conveys: Structure and priority; easy reading.
options.vs: Emphasize accents one item momentarily; hierarchy is the persistent ordering of all items.
options.prompt: Encode hierarchy in choreography: primary element enters first with the longest duration and largest travel, secondary 150-250ms later with 60% travel, tertiary items last with a tight stagger and minimal travel; parents always move before their children.

options.what: Reveals that elements are connected, grouped or belong together.
options.looks: Connector lines draw between nodes, grouped items move together, shared color flashes across related items.
options.motion: Line draw-ons between elements, grouped items sharing one tween, synchronized highlights.
options.use: Integrations, knowledge graphs, system diagrams, feature ecosystems, team and data relationships.
options.conveys: Connectedness, ecosystem, coherence.
options.vs: Show cause and effect adds direction and time; relationship can be symmetric and static once shown.
options.prompt: Show relationships by motion grouping: draw 1.5px connector lines between related elements with stroke-dashoffset, move grouped items with one shared tween (same ease, same start), and flash related items with the same accent color simultaneously.

options.what: Keeps the viewer oriented across a change by carrying elements through it instead of cutting.
options.looks: A shared element persists between scenes, the camera travels continuously, one object becomes the next scene's container.
options.motion: Shared-element transitions, match moves, continuous camera, transform rather than exit-and-enter.
options.use: One-take product films, onboarding flows, UI navigation, temporal composition.
options.conveys: Seamlessness, a coherent system, 'it all fits together'.
options.vs: Show location orients in space (where am I); continuity preserves identity through time (this is the same thing).
options.prompt: Carry at least one element (a card, a shape, a color field, a cursor) across every scene change: tween it from its old position and size to its role in the new scene while the rest of the scene changes around it; avoid hard resets.

options.what: Tells the viewer where something is in a space, a map, a hierarchy or an interface.
options.looks: Zoom out to show context then zoom in, pins drop on maps, breadcrumbs highlight, panels slide from their spatial direction.
options.motion: Zoom-out/zoom-in pairs, directional slides consistent with a spatial model, map camera moves.
options.use: Map animations, navigation demos, infinite-canvas products, multi-panel UIs.
options.conveys: Orientation and scale; the viewer knows where they are.
options.vs: Show navigation is the act of moving between places; location is the orientation that tells you where you are.
options.prompt: Establish location with a context shot: zoom out (scale to 0.4-0.6) to show the whole space and highlight the target region, then zoom back in to it over 800-1200ms; keep directions consistent (deeper levels come from the right or inward).

options.what: Makes the change from one state to another (off to on, empty to full, draft to published) visible and understandable.
options.looks: Toggle knob travels and track recolors, status pill changes color and label, a card flips to its completed side.
options.motion: Color and position tweens on controls, label swaps via vertical roll, icon morphs.
options.use: Settings, workflows, feature toggles, before/after, publish and deploy flows.
options.conveys: Control and clarity; the system's state is always legible.
options.vs: Feedback acknowledges input; state change shows the result. Morph is one technique for showing it.
options.prompt: Animate state changes explicitly: move the control (toggle knob x, checkbox stroke draw), recolor its track or fill over 200-300ms, and roll the status label vertically (old text yPercent 0 to -100, new text 100 to 0) inside an overflow-hidden wrapper.

options.what: Communicates how far a process has advanced toward completion.
options.looks: Progress bars filling, rings closing, step indicators lighting up, percentage counters rising.
options.motion: scaleX fills, stroke-dashoffset ring draws, counters, stepwise highlight.
options.use: Uploads, onboarding steps, deploys, goal tracking, multi-step flows.
options.conveys: Momentum and predictability.
options.vs: Show loading communicates waiting without a known end; progress shows measurable advancement.
options.prompt: Show progress with measurable fills: a bar scaling on x from transform-origin left, or a ring drawn with stroke-dashoffset, synchronized with a counting percentage; advance in uneven chunks (fast, pause, fast) for realism, then land on 100% with a small completion accent.

options.what: Indicates that the system is working and the viewer should wait, with no specific end point shown.
options.looks: Spinners, pulsing skeleton screens, shimmer sweeps across placeholder blocks, typing indicators.
options.motion: Loops: rotation, shimmer gradient translating across, pulse opacity on skeleton blocks.
options.use: AI generation, API requests, data fetching demos, moments of suspense before a result.
options.conveys: Activity, anticipation; in product films keep it brief so the product feels fast.
options.vs: Show progress has a measurable end; loading is indeterminate. Build anticipation is narrative suspense; loading is a system state.
options.prompt: Show loading with a skeleton: placeholder bars in the layout's exact positions, a diagonal light shimmer (a linear-gradient translating xPercent -100 to 100, 1200ms, repeat) across them, or a three-dot typing pulse; keep loading under 1.5s in a product film, then transform the skeleton into the real content.

options.what: Confirms that an action completed as intended.
options.looks: Check marks drawing on, green fills, confetti bursts, badges popping, a satisfying settle.
options.motion: Stroke draw-on check, a small overshoot scale on the badge, a brief burst of particles, color fill.
options.use: Payments, completed tasks, deploys, sign-up, feature payoffs at the end of a demo.
options.conveys: Satisfaction, reward, reliability.
options.vs: Show state change is neutral; success is the positive, celebratory end state.
options.prompt: Celebrate success proportionally: draw a check mark stroke (stroke-dashoffset to 0) over 300-400ms inside a circle that fills with the success color, add a single scale accent to 1.08 and back, and optionally 8-16 small particles bursting outward; no more than one celebration per piece.

options.what: Communicates that an action failed or something is wrong.
options.looks: A horizontal shake, red outline, error icon, a field that refuses input, glitch on a failing system.
options.motion: Short horizontal shake (3-4 oscillations, 6-10px), color change to error red, a stop in otherwise flowing motion.
options.use: Problem framing in problem/solution films, security products, error handling demos, before states.
options.conveys: Friction, risk, the pain the product removes.
options.vs: Show success is its opposite; glitchy motion language is an aesthetic, failure is a meaning.
options.prompt: Show failure with a horizontal refusal shake (x: 0, -8, 8, -6, 6, 0 over 300-400ms), an outline recolor to error red, and an error icon that appears without celebration; in problem/solution films let failure beats be slower and heavier than the solution beats.

options.what: Depicts moving between screens, pages, sections or levels of an interface.
options.looks: Screens push left and right, drill-down zooms, tabs slide an indicator, modals rise over content.
options.motion: Directional push/slide consistent with the information architecture, zoom for depth, indicator slides.
options.use: App walkthroughs, onboarding flows, multi-screen product demos.
options.conveys: Structure of the product, ease of getting around.
options.vs: Show location orients; navigation moves. Transitions (dimension) are editorial scene joins; navigation is diegetic movement inside the product.
options.prompt: Model navigation spatially: forward navigation pushes the current screen out to the left (xPercent -30, dimmed) while the new one slides in from the right; drilling down scales into the tapped element; back reverses exactly; tab changes slide a single indicator bar between tabs.

options.what: Animates values changing so the viewer sees the delta, not just the new number.
options.looks: Bars grow or shrink, lines redraw to new values, numbers count up or roll, rankings reorder.
options.motion: Tweening data attributes (height, path, value), rolling digits, FLIP reorders, delta badges.
options.use: Analytics products, financial results, growth stories, dashboards.
options.conveys: Impact, growth, measurable results.
options.vs: Show progress tracks one process to completion; data change compares values over time or between states.
options.prompt: Animate the delta: tween bar heights and line paths from old values to new values (never redraw from zero), count numbers with a proxy object and snap to integers, add a delta badge (+32%) that appears once the change completes, and reorder ranked items with FLIP position tweens.

options.what: Creates tension before a reveal or payoff so the payoff lands harder.
options.looks: Slow push-ins, elements gathering toward a center, a pause, a teaser glimpse, a riser-driven build.
options.motion: Acceleration toward a moment, contraction before expansion, a whole-frame pause right before the reveal.
options.use: Launch film climaxes, logo reveals, feature unveilings, countdowns.
options.conveys: Excitement, importance of what comes next.
options.vs: The anticipation principle is a small wind-up on one object; build anticipation is a scene-level narrative function.
options.prompt: Build anticipation over 1.5-3s before the payoff: contract elements toward the center (scale 1 to 0.9, gathering), accelerate a camera push with an ease-in, then hold the whole frame still for 300-600ms before the reveal fires at full speed.

options.what: Uses motion primarily to express brand character: humor, confidence, calm or edge.
options.looks: Idle wiggles, a mascot reacting, a logo that winks, a signature ease used everywhere.
options.motion: Signature moves repeated consistently: one characteristic ease, one recurring gesture, idle loops with character.
options.use: Brand identity systems, mascot-led explainers, app personality moments, idents.
options.conveys: Memorability, a recognizable brand voice in motion.
options.vs: Decorate adds motion for visual interest with no voice; personality motion is recognizable and repeatable as brand.
options.prompt: Define one signature move (for example: every card tilts 4deg and settles; the logo mark rotates 90deg on each beat) and one signature ease, and repeat them consistently across every scene so the motion itself becomes recognizable brand language.

options.what: Motion that adds visual richness or atmosphere without carrying information.
options.looks: Drifting gradients, floating particles, background shapes rotating, grain shimmer, parallax background layers.
options.motion: Slow ambient loops at low amplitude and contrast, below the functional layer.
options.use: Backgrounds, hero loops, ambient screens, filling holds in title sequences.
options.conveys: Atmosphere and polish; in excess, noise that competes with content.
options.vs: Create personality carries brand voice; decorate is atmosphere only. It should never move faster or with higher contrast than the functional layer.
options.prompt: Keep decorative motion ambient: loops of 6-20s, amplitudes under 5% of frame size, contrast at least 40% lower than content, sine.inOut or constant drift; pause or dim decoration whenever a functional animation plays.
